topics.title: Why NumPy exists
topics.body: A Python loop adds one number at a time and pays interpreter overhead per element; NumPy performs the same addition in compiled code over a contiguous buffer. That is the reason numerical work starts with an array, not a list.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
marks = [40, 55, 70, 85]
a = np.array(marks)
print(a.sum(), a.mean())
print(a.dtype, a.shape)

topics.title: An array versus a list
topics.body: A list can mix a string, a float and a nested list; an ndarray holds one dtype and reports one shape. Mixing types in an array silently promotes them all to a common dtype.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
mixed = np.array([1, 2.5, True])
print(mixed, mixed.dtype)

topics.title: Every attribute of an ndarray
topics.body: shape, ndim, size, dtype, itemsize and nbytes answer different questions about the same buffer, and strides tells you how many elements each axis step moves.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)
print(a.shape, a.ndim, a.size, a.dtype, a.itemsize, a.nbytes, a.strides)

topics.title: np.empty is not filled with zeros
topics.body: empty allocates the buffer without writing values, so whatever was in memory is what you read. Use zeros when you need a known starting value.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
z = np.zeros(3, dtype=np.int64)
print(z, z.dtype)
print(np.zeros((2, 2)).shape)

topics.title: arange versus linspace
topics.body: arange takes a step and can miss the stop value; linspace takes a count and always includes both ends. For floats, linspace is usually the safer choice.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 1, 0.25))
print(np.linspace(0, 1, 5))

topics.title: Identity and eye
topics.body: eye builds an identity of any rectangular shape, while identity requires a square one. Both put ones on the main diagonal.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.eye(3, dtype=int))
print(np.identity(2, dtype=int))

topics.title: Casting a float to an integer truncates
topics.body: astype does not round; it drops the fractional part toward zero. Convert after rounding when the value should not lose precision.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.9, -1.9, 2.5])
print(a.astype(np.int64))
print(np.round(a).astype(np.int64))

topics.title: Type promotion with result_type
topics.body: When two dtypes meet in an operation NumPy promotes to one that can hold both. result_type tells you which dtype that will be before you compute anything.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.result_type(np.int32, np.float32))
print((np.array([1], dtype=np.int8) + 0.5).dtype)

topics.title: Rows, columns and single cells
topics.body: In a 2-D array the first index picks the row and the second the column, so a[1] is a row, a[:, 1] is a column and a[1, 2] is one cell.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a[1])
print(a[:, 1])
print(a[1, 2])

topics.title: Ellipsis and newaxis
topics.body: Ellipsis stands for every axis you did not name, and newaxis inserts a length-one axis so a 1-D array can broadcast against a 2-D one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(24).reshape(2, 3, 4)
print(a[..., 0].shape)
print(np.array([1, 2, 3])[np.newaxis, :].shape)

topics.title: Writing through a slice edits the original
topics.body: Slicing returns a view of the same buffer, so writing through the slice changes the original. Use copy when the two must be independent.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
b = a[1:4]
b[0] = 99
print(a, b)

topics.title: Reverse with a negative step
topics.body: A step of -1 walks the axis backwards and keeps the shape otherwise unchanged. The same syntax works per axis on a 2-D array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
print(a[::-1])
print(np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])[::-1, ::-1])

topics.title: reshape returns a view when it can
topics.body: reshape never copies if the existing strides allow the new shape; ravel returns a view where possible and a copy otherwise. Use flatten when a copy is required.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
b = a.reshape(2, 3)
b[0, 0] = 99
print(a, b.shape)

topics.title: Stack and concatenate
topics.body: concatenate joins along an existing axis, vstack adds rows and hstack adds columns. stack creates a new axis instead of joining one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2])
b = np.array([3, 4])
print(np.vstack([a, b]))
print(np.hstack([a, b]))
print(np.stack([a, b]).shape)

topics.title: reduce and accumulate
topics.body: add.reduce collapses an axis to one value, while add.accumulate keeps every running total. They are ufunc methods, so they work with any binary ufunc.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(np.add.reduce(a))
print(np.add.accumulate(a))

topics.title: Never compare floats with ==
topics.body: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimals exactly, so two computations that should agree can differ in the last bits. isclose compares within a tolerance instead.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(np.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))

topics.title: A column broadcasts against a row
topics.body: Shape (3, 1) against (1, 4) stretches both to (3, 4): each row value meets each column value. That single rule is how standardising every column is written without a loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
col = np.array([[10], [20], [30]])
row = np.array([[1, 2, 3, 4]])
print(col + row)

topics.title: expand_dims adds the axis explicitly
topics.body: expand_dims is the function form of newaxis: it inserts a length-one axis at the position you name, which makes the intended broadcast shape obvious in code.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a.shape, np.expand_dims(a, 0).shape, np.expand_dims(a, 1).shape)

topics.title: axis=0 sums columns, axis=1 sums rows
topics.body: The axis you name is the axis that disappears. Summing a (2, 3) array with axis=0 collapses the rows and leaves one value per column.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a.sum(axis=0), a.sum(axis=0).shape)
print(a.sum(axis=1), a.sum(axis=1).shape)

topics.title: Percentiles answer rank questions
topics.body: percentile returns the value below which a percentage of the data falls, using linear interpolation by default. It is the number to quote for latency and marks, not the mean.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([12, 15, 18, 22, 30, 41])
print(np.percentile(a, 50), np.percentile(a, [25, 75]))

topics.title: where chooses between two arrays
topics.body: np.where(condition, x, y) returns x where the condition is true and y where it is false, which replaces an if/else loop over the elements.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
marks = np.array([35, 72, 48, 90])
print(np.where(marks >= 50, 'pass', 'fail'))

topics.title: Updating through a mask
topics.body: A boolean mask can be used on the left of an assignment, so only the selected cells change and the rest keep their values.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([-5, 3, -2, 8])
a[a < 0] = 0
print(a)

topics.title: argsort gives positions, sort gives values
topics.body: argsort returns the indices that would sort the array, which is what you need to reorder a second array the same way.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
names = np.array(['b', 'a', 'c'])
score = np.array([2, 9, 5])
order = np.argsort(score)
print(order, names[order], score[order])

topics.title: Set operations on arrays
topics.body: intersect1d, union1d and setdiff1d treat the arrays as sets and return sorted unique values, which is how duplicate detection and reconciliation are written.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 3])
b = np.array([3, 4])
print(np.intersect1d(a, b))
print(np.union1d(a, b))
print(np.setdiff1d(a, b))

topics.title: itemsize and nbytes
topics.body: itemsize is the bytes one element occupies and nbytes is itemsize times size. Changing dtype changes both without changing shape.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros(5, dtype=np.int32)
b = np.zeros(5, dtype=np.float64)
print(a.itemsize, a.nbytes, b.itemsize, b.nbytes)

topics.title: C order and Fortran order
topics.body: C order walks the last axis fastest, Fortran order the first. The flags say which layout a buffer uses, and ascontiguousarray gives you the C layout.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.flags['C_CONTIGUOUS'], a.strides)
print(a.T.flags['C_CONTIGUOUS'], a.T.strides)

topics.title: A seed makes randomness repeatable
topics.body: Two generators built with the same seed produce the same stream, which is how an experiment becomes reproducible. A different seed gives a different stream.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
r1 = np.random.default_rng(42)
r2 = np.random.default_rng(42)
print(r1.random(3))
print(r2.random(3))

topics.title: Choice with and without replacement
topics.body: rng.choice samples from a list; replace=False samples without repeating an item, which is what a shuffled train/test split needs.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
print(rng.choice([10, 20, 30, 40], size=2, replace=False))
print(rng.permutation(5))

topics.title: Matrix multiplication with @
topics.body: The @ operator contracts the last axis of the left operand with the second-to-last of the right. Elementwise * is a different operation with a different result.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
b = np.array([[5, 6], [7, 8]])
print(a @ b)
print(a * b)

topics.title: Solve, do not invert
topics.body: np.linalg.solve(A, b) solves Ax = b directly and is more stable and faster than computing inv(A) @ b. Inversion also loses accuracy on ill-conditioned matrices.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[3.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0]])
b = np.array([9.0, 8.0])
print(np.linalg.solve(a, b))
print(np.linalg.det(a))

topics.title: save and load one array
topics.body: save writes a .npy file that keeps dtype and shape, and load reads it back exactly. Unlike CSV, no text conversion happens.
topics.code:
import numpy as np, tempfile, os
a = np.arange(4, dtype=np.float32)
p = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), 'a.npy')
np.save(p, a)
b = np.load(p)
print(b, b.dtype, b.shape)

topics.title: savez stores several arrays
topics.body: savez groups named arrays into one .npz archive, and load returns a mapping you index by name. Use savez_compressed for large, repetitive data.
topics.code:
import numpy as np, tempfile, os
a, b = np.arange(3), np.ones((2, 2))
p = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), 'pack.npz')
np.savez(p, first=a, second=b)
z = np.load(p)
print(sorted(z.files), z['second'].shape)

topics.title: Dates as datetime64
topics.body: datetime64 stores an instant on a fixed unit, so subtraction gives a timedelta64 and comparison is a number comparison. No timezone is carried.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
d = np.array(['2026-01-01', '2026-03-01'], dtype='datetime64[D]')
print(d, d[1] - d[0])
print(d + np.timedelta64(10, 'D'))

topics.title: Structured arrays hold named fields
topics.body: A structured dtype gives every row named, typed fields, so a record stays one row instead of three parallel arrays.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rec = np.array([(1, 92.5), (2, 81.0)], dtype=[('id', 'i4'), ('score', 'f8')])
print(rec['score'].mean(), rec.dtype.names)

topics.title: Masked arrays ignore invalid cells
topics.body: A masked array carries a mask beside the data, so reductions skip the masked positions instead of returning NaN.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
import numpy.ma as ma
a = ma.array([1, 2, 3], mask=[False, True, False])
print(a.mean(), a.filled(0))

topics.title: nan_to_num replaces non-finite values
topics.body: NaN and infinity break arithmetic and sorting. nan_to_num maps them to chosen finite values so downstream code has no special cases.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([np.nan, np.inf, -np.inf, 2.0])
print(np.nan_to_num(a, nan=0.0, posinf=1e9, neginf=-1e9))

topics.title: Avoid temporaries with out=
topics.body: Every expression allocates a new array. Passing out= writes into an existing buffer, which matters when the arrays are large and the loop is repeated.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4.0)
out = np.empty_like(a)
np.multiply(a, 2, out=out)
print(out, out is a)

topics.title: In-place operations save memory
topics.body: Operators ending in = update the buffer instead of allocating, so a += 1 costs no new array. The trade-off is that aliased views see the change.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones(4, dtype=np.int64)
before = a
before += 1
print(a, before is a)

topics.title: An image is just an array
topics.body: A colour image is a (height, width, 3) array, so slicing a channel is plain indexing and brightness is multiplication by a scalar.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
img = np.arange(12).reshape(2, 2, 3)
print(img.shape)
print(img[..., 0])
print((img * 0).shape)

topics.title: Moving between NumPy and the rest of Python
topics.body: asarray accepts lists and tuples without copying when it can, and tolist returns plain lists for JSON or an API. That boundary is where dtype and shape must be checked.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
data = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
a = np.asarray(data)
print(a.shape, a.dtype, a.tolist())
